This page corresponds to the precise U.S. O*NET/SOC 17-2112.01 occupation "Human Factors Engineers and Ergonomists" (human factors engineers and ergonomists): designing objects, facilities, and environments to optimize human well-being and overall system performance by applying theory, principles, and data regarding the relationship between humans and technology, and investigating and analyzing characteristics of human behavior and performance as they relate to the use of technology. Official scope text: Design objects, facilities, and environments to optimize human well-being and overall system performance, applying theory, principles, and data regarding the relationship between humans and respective technology. Investigate and analyze characteristics of human behavior and performance as it relates to the use of technology. The U.S. wages and employment on this page come from BLS OEWS 2025 and BLS employment projections 2024—2034 as presented by O*NET, and O*NET labels both datasets as the Industrial Engineers combined scope; the precise occupational wage for mainland China was not obtained and is registered as a visible gap; the two jurisdictions and their occupational safety systems must not be applied to one another.

To judge whether human factors engineering and ergonomics suits you, first run one verifiable human factors assessment drill using public or simulated materials: choose a fictional work scenario (for example, an assembly workstation where repetitive movements cause fatigue and errors), and write a process from clarifying system and user goals, observing work activities and collecting data, interviewing or surveying to understand needs and fatigue, performing functional and anthropometric analyses, identifying physical and cognitive risks, proposing improvements, to producing a report and validating effects, marking the method and evidence type at each step and the possible abnormalities (insufficient data, sample bias, site constraints, conflicts between improvements and safety or compliance, stakeholder disagreement). Afterward, check: whether observation and data evidence and privacy and informed consent are treated as non-omittable items; whether safety determinations or compliance conclusions beyond your authority are written as requests for guidance or for decision by qualified personnel; and whether uncertainty is written into the report. Test with a real deliverable, not just answers to an interest questionnaire.

Fit signals | The work activities for U.S. O*NET 17-2112.01 show that getting information, making decisions and solving problems, identifying objects, actions, and events, communicating with colleagues, analyzing data or information, and using computers are the most important activities for this occupation; work context shows that electronic mail 95% report every day, telephone conversations 74% report every day, face-to-face discussions 63% report every day, freedom to make decisions 60% report a lot of freedom, indoors, environmentally controlled 61% report every day, contact with others 50% report most of the time, importance of being exact or accurate 47% report very important, and typical work week 55% report 40 hours. The most important skills include active listening, critical thinking, reading comprehension, speaking, and writing. If you are willing to design solutions based on observation, measurement, and data analysis, and to persuade people from different specialties with reports, these daily demands are closer to the way you work.

Caution signals | O*NET also shows (17-2112.01): importance of being exact or accurate 47% report very important, time pressure 50% report once a week or more, competition 50% report highly competitive, very high responsibility for others' health and safety 35%, and contact with others 50% report most of the time. This occupation deals with human behavior and performance data, physical and cognitive safety, and system design recommendations: a single misuse of a measurement or statistical method, a single inference that treats correlation as causation, a single improvement recommendation that ignores site constraints, or a single safety determination beyond your authority can produce wrong conclusions or make an improvement fail when implemented. This page therefore lists data and method quality, site constraints and verifiability, and the authorization boundaries of safety and compliance separately. On the U.S. side, this occupation is marked Bright Outlook, and the O*NET page shows the related combined scope (Industrial Engineers) is projected to grow far above average (11%) from 2024 to 2034, with about 25,200 job openings per year and employment of about 351,100 in 2024, but those data are the Industrial Engineers combined scope and do not equal this occupation's precise size. If it is hard for you to sustain long periods of seated analytical work, cross-specialty communication, or having recommendations rejected, you should treat these as real costs that need careful weighing.

Commitment judgment | Real fit comes from whether you can do three things in the same assessment at once: make the human factors assessment solid (clarify goals, collect observation and measurement data, perform functional and anthropometric analyses, and propose and validate improvements, producing a report whose methods can be reproduced); keep data and boundaries under control (method applicability, privacy and informed consent, site and safety constraints, and handing safety determinations beyond your authority to qualified personnel); and carry definable professional responsibility (be responsible for the rigor of your own methods and conclusions, and disclose uncertainty and limitations truthfully). It is recommended to test this with one verifiable experience (completing a step-by-step human factors assessment process and draft report, or a drill on recognizing and handling common human factors problems), rather than relying only on the conclusions of an interest questionnaire.

The daily work of human factors engineers and ergonomists can be broken down along three lines: (1) research and data—observing work activities, interviews and surveys, and functional and anthropometric analyses to form a reproducible data foundation; (2) design and recommendations—proposing improvements to objects, facilities, environments, interfaces, or processes based on data, and advocating for end users; (3) reports and collaboration—writing reports and presentations, collaborating with engineers, designers, and managers, and providing technical support to clients. The three lines share the same set of method and evidence requirements, but their deliverables go to different recipients: research and data serve the evidence, design and recommendations serve the solution, and reports and collaboration serve decisions and implementation.

O*NET 17-2112.01 "Human Factors Engineers and Ergonomists": using theory and data on the human-technology relationship to design objects, facilities, and environments that optimize human well-being and overall system performance, and investigating and analyzing characteristics of human behavior and performance as they relate to the use of technology. Core tasks are observing and collecting data, interviews and surveys, advocating for end users, inspecting workplaces to identify hazards, performing functional and anthropometric analyses, recommending improvements, and writing reports. Job Zone Level Five (extensive preparation needed).

entries: Data collection | Observing work activities and collecting data | Collect data by directly observing work activities or witnessing test processes, and identify and classify relevant objects, actions, and events (O*NET task: collecting data by observation).

User research | Understanding needs through interviews and surveys | Interview or survey users or customers to collect information on needs, fatigue, human factors, and interfaces (O*NET task: conducting interviews or surveys).

User advocacy | Speaking for end users | Work with other professionals (engineers, designers, managers, or customers) to advocate for end users' needs and experience (O*NET task: advocating for end users).

Risk assessment | Inspecting workplaces to identify hazards | Inspect workplaces to identify physical hazards, and recommend improvements to health and safety based on harmful factors such as heavy loads or repetitive motions (O*NET tasks: inspecting workplaces to identify physical hazards; recommending improvements to health and safety).

Analysis and measurement | Functional and anthropometric analysis | Perform functional, task, or anthropometric analyses using tools such as checklists, questionnaires, video, or force measurement (O*NET task: performing functional, task, or anthropometric analyses).

Reports and support | Writing reports and providing technical support | Write reports or presentations summarizing the results and conclusions of tests, investigations, or validation, and provide clients with human factors or ergonomics technical support (O*NET tasks: writing reports or presentations; providing technical support).

subject.name: Human Factors Engineers and Ergonomists
subject.summary: Human factors engineers and ergonomists corresponds to the precise U.S. O*NET/SOC 17-2112.01 occupation "Human Factors Engineers and Ergonomists": designing objects, facilities, and environments to optimize human well-being and overall system performance by applying theory, principles, and data regarding the relationship between humans and technology, and investigating and analyzing characteristics of human behavior and performance as they relate to the use of technology. Official scope text: Design objects, facilities, and environments to optimize human well-being and overall system performance, applying theory, principles, and data regarding the relationship between humans and respective technology. Investigate and analyze characteristics of human behavior and performance as it relates to the use of technology. Core tasks include observing work activities and testing to collect data, conducting interviews or surveys, advocating for end users, inspecting workplaces to identify physical hazards, performing functional and anthropometric analyses, and recommending improvements and writing reports. The U.S. wages and employment on this page come from BLS OEWS 2025 and BLS employment projections 2024—2034 as presented by O*NET, and O*NET labels both datasets as the Industrial Engineers combined scope; the precise occupational wage for mainland China was not obtained and is registered as a visible gap; China's engineering qualification and safety institutional boundaries are labeled separately.
